en: In the *Munimatālaṃkāra*, it is asked: "Now, regarding that which was stated—that there is arising conventionally (*saṃvṛtyā*)—what is this so-called 'convention' (*saṃvṛti*)?

(1) It is said that convention is the deluded cognition which, despite things being devoid of intrinsic nature, superimposes an erroneous form upon them as if they were real entities. This is because reality is concealed (*saṃvriyate*) or covered up by it, or within it.
And so it is said in the Sūtra: "Entities arise conventionally; in the ultimate sense, they are without intrinsic nature.
The delusion regarding those things that lack intrinsic nature is considered conventional reality (*tathyasaṃvṛti*)."
Thus, because they exist [only] as such, all these entities shown here are called "conventional" (*sāṃvṛta*), being false.

And that [conventionality] arises for all living beings by virtue of the maturation of the beginningless latencies of delusion, presenting non-existent entities as if they were existent; therefore, from the perspective of intention, everything...
Thus, phenomena that are false in nature are called "conventionally existent";
however, they do not possess the nature of being real entities in an ultimate sense, because their mode of appearance is not their true reality.
Nor does it have the nature of absolute non-existence, like the horn of a hare, because it appears in a form that is charming so long as it is not investigated.

For instance, just as a form established by people possessing deluded cognition in the case of a magical illusion or the like is so perceived, so too, that which is superimposed upon all things by cognitions of false forms is designated as conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*).

And in that very same way, just as a form established by those with unimpaired consciousness in the case of a magical illusion or the like, so too, that form of all things which is definitively determined by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).

And just as, based on the two truths— the conventional and the ultimate— as established by the cognitions of the deluded and the undeluded, the Vijñānavādins' distinction that things such as hair perceived by those with cataracts exist conventionally but do not exist ultimately, and so forth, regarding the duality of subject and object, does not involve contradiction due to the difference in perspective,
so it is likewise for all categories of entities.

Therefore, conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*), which consists of the aforementioned error, displays even non-arisen entities as if they were arising in actuality; because of that, by virtue of its basis, entities arise conventionally, yet in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*) they do not arise.
Because its object is the non-erroneous reality, all knowledge consisting of correct hearing, reflection, and cultivation is called "ultimate" (paramārtha),
on the grounds that this [reality] is its supreme object.
The distinction, however, is whether [the realization] is produced directly or through a lineage.
By virtue of that, all these phenomena are perceived as being indeed unarisen;
what is meant is that their arising is not established by correct cognition.
Or, conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*) is that which is without investigation (*avicāra*).

For, the wisdom consisting of reflection (*cintāmayī prajñā*)— which arises through the power of correct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) engaged in the contemplation of non-erroneous reality— and likewise the wisdom consisting of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī*), are called "investigation" because they either directly investigate the meaning of reality or are its natural outflow (*niṣyanda*).
Thus, all cognition that is turned away from the object and, by its very opposite, grasps a false appearance, is non-investigative (*avicāra*);
it is neither non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka-jñāna*) nor merely the absence of investigation.
Therefore, because it possesses a form established through such [non-investigative] means, every entity that has a false form is conventional (*sāṃvṛta*).
Alternatively, conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*) is worldly consensus (*lokapratīti*),

because every object established by the entire world is accepted as being conventional. Furthermore, not every object is the domain of every sense faculty, since some objects are perceived only by certain [faculties].

Therefore, the establishment of things that are absolutely beyond the senses—such as the specific results of actions corresponding to their various modes—is possible only through the knowledge of an omniscient being; for other matters, however, it may be established even by the knowledge of others.

Furthermore, whatever form of permanence or other characteristics of entities has been postulated by certain authors of treatises in defiance of common experience is called a false conventional reality (*mithyā-saṃvṛti-sat*),
because it does not exist even according to experience.
On the other hand, that which is postulated in accordance with experience—
For example, [the statement] "There is no sentient being or self here; rather, these phenomena exist with their causes" is called a true conventional reality (*tathyasaṃvṛtisat*).

Therefore, even though multiple forms are superimposed upon a single entity by the authors of treatises, it does not follow that the entity possesses multiple mutually contradictory intrinsic natures.
Alternatively, the meaning of "illusion" (māyā) is the meaning of "conventional reality" (saṃvṛti).
The meaning of "illusion" is the meaning of "unreal.
Furthermore, even though the object of illusion is of the nature of deluded cognition, it does not follow that the cognition itself possesses substantial reality.
Because that [object] appears by assuming a false form, and because the real and the false forms are mutually contradictory,
it would follow that even the false form possesses reality; thus, the cognition would not be erroneous.
Nor can it have a variegated form, because that would involve a contradiction.
Alternatively, if it were erroneous, then because even its unreal form would be false, the cognition itself could not be real.
This is because the two are in every respect non-different from one another, and thus it is impossible for there to be a relationship of part and whole between them.
Therefore, since cognition too would be false, this [system] differs greatly from the doctrine of internal objects of cognition (*antarjñeyanaya*).
Those who are ignorant claim that "mere sound" (*śabdamātra*) is the conventional (*saṃvṛti*).
For no follower of the Sugata holds the view that mere sound is the conventional. As it is said: "All this is name-only; it is established in mere designation."
Apart from the designation, the designated object does not exist.
Thus it is stated in the Sūtra; therein,

for the purpose of refuting the view of those who imagine that the signifier and the signified are real entities existing as distinct from one another, it is demonstrated that both the signifier and the signified are not established through conceptual construction (*kalpanā*).
For in this context, "perception" (*saṃjñā*) means conceptual construction (*kalpanā*).
What is intended by the term "name" (*nāman*) is precisely that which has the form of conceptual construction;
it does not refer to the object appearing to auditory cognition, because that [object] is not expressive.
And if the universe were merely that [consciousness], there would be no manifestation of the diversity of forms and so forth,
nor would there be the differentiation into aggregates and the like.
Just as among many illusory persons, the referent of a word is established as a conceptualized common form— namely, "person" in the sense of "person"— so too,

even though things lack an intrinsic nature in the ultimate sense, when the ultimate is spoken of by way of a superimposed form, it would be merely conventional, because the ultimate transcends all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).

And so it is said in the Sūtra: "O Devaputra, if ultimate truth were to come within the range of body, speech, and mind from the perspective of ultimate reality, it would not be reckoned as 'ultimate truth';
it would merely be conventional truth.
Rather, from the perspective of ultimate reality, ultimate truth transcends all conventional designations."
Thus.
Alternatively, the momentariness of phenomena is the conventional truth.
The ultimate truth is the emptiness characterized by the lack of intrinsic nature, which is the illusory nature of all those phenomena that are mobile by essence;
it is eternal because it remains established at all times, whether Tathāgatas arise or do not arise. (6)
